title: Update: People who knew shooter believe he suffered from mental health issues
article: The gunman who fired multiple rounds out of a Huntington Hills home before he was fatally shot by police on Sunday was confined to a wheelchair and complained online about his neighbours, the government, and police.

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team is investigating after police tore through the back fence of a home near 78th Avenue and 10th Street N.W. late Sunday afternoon and shot David McQueen, who was armed with a handgun, when he exited the back of his home in his wheelchair shortly after 6 p.m.
Police Chief Roger Chaffin said shots were fired "indiscriminately" from a man in the home beginning around 4:40 p.m., and a bullet narrowly missed striking a Calgary Transit bus driver.
"The suspect in this case was actively engaging us and the neighbourhood with a firearm," Chaffin said on Monday morning.
"We were very concerned about the wellbeing of our officers and the public."
McQueen, 53, broke his neck after diving headfirst into shallow Sikome Lake in 1994 while at the popular Calgary watering hole with his sons.
In 2001, a judge ruled McQueen, a paraplegic, was at fault for the injuries he sustained after he launched a $4-million lawsuit against the province.

McQueen identified himself online as a quadriplegic and in recent years, he found support in a beloved black service dog named Bear, who died earlier this month, according to McQueen's Facebook posts.

In lengthy online posts, McQueen detailed perceived mistreatment by the healthcare system, government and lawyers, and he accused his neighbours of stalking him and the police of threatening to shoot his dog.
Dino Chiodo, an ex-brother-in-law, said he last spoke to McQueen three months ago, and was concerned, as McQueen seemed slightly paranoid.
"He thought people were spying on him," Chiodo said. "Dave was an amazing baseball player in his youth and he probably could have done anything he wanted to do...
"Since then he had some bad luck in life, and he became an incomplete quadriplegic. But he's always been a compassionate, thoughtful person who cared a lot about other people.
"It's unbelievable that it's come to this."
Police had been to McQueen's home before Sunday's fatal shooting but wouldn't elaborate on why.
"Our experience with the shooter had been sort of in the non-criminal nature," said Chaffin. "We didn't have any particular experience with him in terms of this level of violence."

David Swann, interim Liberal leader and the MLA for Calgary-Mountain View, said McQueen had frequently reached out to his constituency office and appeared to be deeply troubled. He was angry with his injury and with "a system he felt failed him, and angry with those who represented that system," Swann said in a statement.
"He was suffering from an obvious, and serious, mental illness and it was often difficult to understand where he was coming from or how we could help.

"He was always polite, though he was certainly agitated and paranoid of all government," Swann said, adding he was thinking about people, "like my staff, who interacted with Mr. McQueen and are left, today, feeling they could have done more."

Police were first alerted to the incident when a bus driver called 911 around 4:40 p.m. Sunday to report that his bus, which contained five passengers, was hit by gunfire while parked at a Huntington Hills bus stop.
At least a dozen officers, including tactical team members, descended on the northwest neighbourhood and officers set up containment while shots continued to be fired from the home.
Officers urged residents in the area to hunker down in their basements for an extended period of time as they addressed the situation, which Chaffin said intensified after the suspect left his home.
"Several attempts were made to resolve the situation peacefully," the police chief said.
"However, the suspect exited the residence and the situation escalated resulting in a discharge of a service firearm resulting in killing the suspect."
Police tried to talk to McQueen before the fatal confrontation but were unsuccessful.
"The continuous amount of engagement that we were experiencing led to the ultimate confrontation with police," Chaffin said.
"We're fortunate no innocent bystanders were injured."
Chaffin said police don't yet know the shooter's motivation or exactly how many shots were fired.
Neighbour Ed Hall, who has lived across the street from McQueen for 16 years, said recently his wife walked by McQueen's home and heard somebody "banging on the window and yelling at her."
"It really scared her," he said.
"I always thought the guy wasn't right."
Tim Kinzer, who lives around the corner from McQueen said he heard several gunshots late Sunday afternoon and saw McQueen slumped over dead in his wheelchair outside his home.
"As far as I could tell... he was maybe two feet out [from his door] in the wheelchair," he said.
In his 12 years in the neighbourhood, Kinzer had only spoken to McQueen a few times, but he said he could tell McQueen was troubled.
"He was a bit paranoid. He had mental issues, mental problems. He was convinced that some of the neighbours were stalking him and robbing from him," said Kinzer.
"He was a very reclusive person. He only came out once a week, twice a week to go grocery shopping or whatever. In the summertime he would come out on the back deck and enjoy the weather."
McQueen was a former client of Easter Seals, an organization that helps Albertans with physical disabilities, and appeared in one of the group's videos in 2009.
"We are very saddened to hear the news of the passing of Dave McQueen," said Susan Boivin, CEO Easter Seals Alberta.
"He was a former client of Easter Seals' Equipment and Support Services program, but we have not had any contact with him for many years."
Neighbour Calena Kawanami said she broke down in tears when she found out McQueen was killed.
"He's a sweet man," she said.
